units: the takes recorded in the room come out muddy
the engineer blames the hard surfaces of the walls
a sound takes too long to die away in the room
the player reports a hum coming from the air system
the first fix is to hang absorbent material near the microphones
the second fix is to rest the air duct on flexible mounts
the player fears the tone of her instrument will be altered
the engineer promises a gain in the high frequencies instead
text: The studio engineer kept saying that the takes recorded in that room came out muddy, and he laid the blame squarely on the walls. Nothing there soaked up anything: every note hung on far too long, and the wash of it smeared the attack of whatever was being played. The cellist had a complaint of her own. Whenever the air system started up, she could hear a low hum sitting under everything. So the engineer set out two fixes. Hang absorbent panels close behind the microphones, first of all, to break up what the bare surfaces kept throwing back. Then rest the air duct on flexible mounts, so its shudder stopped traveling through the floor. The cellist worried about what all that would do to the tone of her instrument. The engineer told her the opposite would happen: take out the stray echo and the top end comes back, the part the room had been eating.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: two ways of passing music on coexisted over long stretches of time
the first way rests on a pupil copying a master by ear
in that way nothing is set down on any material support
every performer freely alters the piece he has learned
the second way uses written signs giving pitch and duration
writing fixes the work and lets it travel far from its author
transmission by ear breeds many versions
specialists find that the two paths have combined
copyists set down only a framework that performers filled in
text: Over long stretches of time, music traveled by two routes at once, and the contrast between them still shapes how players work today. The first route asked for nothing but the ear. A master played, a pupil copied, and the piece moved on through patient repetition. Nothing was set down on any material support, so every performer bent the tune a little, adding a turn here, cutting a repeat there. The second route used written signs that told the eye how high a note sat and how long it lasted. Writing pinned the work down and let it travel far from whoever had made it. Music carried by ear breeds versions without end. The written page breeds faithful copies. Yet scholars have shown that the two never stood apart. What the copyists set down was a framework, and the players filled in the silence the pages left them.

units: every sound comes from a fast motion that stirs the surrounding air
the first family gathers strings pulled tight between two supports
these strings are set moving by plucking, bowing or striking them
a hollow body strengthens the motion passed on by the string
the second family gathers hollow tubes driven by the breath of the player
the pitch obtained in a tube depends on the length of air left free
the third family gathers skins stretched over a frame
the fourth family gathers metal bars and plates that are struck
each family is known by its tone color, tied to the material used
text: Sound begins with a fast motion that stirs the air around it, and the objects able to make that motion fall into families. In the first are strings pulled tight between two supports. You pluck them, you draw a bow across them, or you strike them, and the shaking passes into a hollow body that strengthens it. The second family is built from open tubes: the breath of the player sets a column of air moving inside, and how high the note sits depends on how much of that column is left free. The third gathers skins stretched over a frame, which answer a blow with a short, dark ring. The fourth holds bars and plates of metal that sound on their own the moment something hits them. Each family has a voice you learn to know, because the material doing the moving filters the overtones in its own way.

units: a neighbor takes the narrator down to the basement of their building one evening
the neighbor claims the pipes give out a kind of song
the two women go down with a lamp and a recorder
at first they hear only the boiler and the metal door
when the pump stops a low held note appears
a faint high sound rides above that low note
the neighbor admits she has been hearing this for several weeks
playing the take back reveals a regular throbbing
a repairman later blames a valve left badly closed
text: One evening the neighbor from the floor below dragged me down to the basement of our building, swearing that the pipes sang down there. We went with a lamp and a borrowed recorder. At first there was nothing worth the trip: the boiler grumbling, the metal door creaking shut behind us. Then the pump cut out, and the whole cellar began to ring. A low note came up out of the plumbing, steady and held, with a thin whistle riding above it. She laughed and owned up that she had been hearing it for weeks without daring to mention it. We let the machine run for half an hour. Playing the take back upstairs, we heard that note plain, throbbing with an even beat that made it tremble. The repairman who came the week after needed one look: a valve left badly closed, a pipe whistling like a flute.

units: capturing the sounds of a street calls for a careful method
you have to pick a spot sheltered from moving air
air striking the microphone membrane makes an overwhelming rumble
the machine has to be clamped to a steady support
a hand holding the microphone passes on audible rubbing
you should switch your phone off to avoid interference
a take should start before the event aimed at and run on past it
you have to listen to the take on headphones before leaving the place
text: Recording a street takes more care than people expect, and every shortcut shows up later in the edit. Pick a sheltered spot first, because moving air slams into the microphone membrane and lays a rumble over everything else. Then clamp the machine to a stand. Hold it in your hand instead and every shift of your fingers turns into a steady scrape running the whole length of the take. Switch your phone off as well, or it can drop a short burst of interference into the file that no amount of cleaning will lift. Start rolling before the thing you came for and keep rolling well past it, or the cut will land too early and the passage will be useless. Last of all, listen on headphones while you are still standing there. A fault caught late means coming back; a fault caught on the spot takes one step sideways to fix.

units: a rail line runs right along the yard of a school
passing trains cover the voices of the children
the teachers describe lessons broken off again and again
protective work was carried out over one season
a thick tilted wall throws the sound wave back toward the track
the windows of the building were given reinforced glazing
absorbent cladding was laid over the exposed face
the noise remains but seems clearly further off
the children now hear the bell without straining
text: Stand in the school yard and the first thing you hear is not the children but the rail line running along the wall. Every so often a train comes through, and the squeal of wheels on the curved rail swallows the voices, the games, the bell itself. Teachers talk about lessons chopped into pieces, dictations started again from the top, pupils raising their voices without noticing. The work took a whole season. A thick wall, tilted toward the track, now throws the wave back down onto the ballast instead of letting it clear the fence. The windows were fitted with reinforced glazing, and absorbent cladding covers the exposed face of the building. The roar has not gone. It has moved off, as though pushed behind a heavy curtain. Out in the yard the bell rides over the voices again, and nobody has to shout to be heard.

units: two rooms in the same music school sound different
the lower room is lined with wood mounted on a hollow frame
its walls drink up the high frequencies and soften the attack
the upper room is built of polished stone and has no drapes
its walls send the sound wave back almost without loss
quick notes pile onto one another there
a brass section gains fullness in the upper room
a string quartet loses clarity there
the teachers keep the lower room for sessions of fine adjustment
text: The lower room and the upper room of the music school do not sound alike, and the ear picks it up in the opening bar. Wood panels line the lower room, mounted on a hollow frame. Those walls give a little with the instrument, drink up the high end, and hand back a warm, faintly veiled sound in which the bite of a bowed string rounds off. Upstairs it is polished stone, with no drapes and no rugs. The walls send the wave back almost whole, so the ring hangs on and quick notes pile onto each other before any of them has died out. A brass section swells there and fills the space, while a string quartet turns cloudy and loses its edge. That is why the teachers keep the lower room for the sessions where fine adjustments get made, and send the larger groups upstairs when what they want is weight.

units: the writer disputes the idea that music played without a break is harmless
he puts forward three objections one after the other
the first objection concerns the drain on the attention of the customer
this drain brings on a tiredness whose cause escapes the person feeling it
the second objection concerns the staff exposed to the same sound loop
these staff have no control at all over what they hear
the third objection concerns the way music itself loses its worth
the writer holds that silence is what makes a sound audible
text: Treating the music that runs without a break in shops as a harmless little comfort is a mistake. Three objections deserve a hearing. The first has to do with attention. An unbroken stream of sound takes a cut of whatever mental resources a customer brings through the door, so he listens without listening and tires out without ever placing the cause. The second concerns the people who work under it. The clerk, the server and the one at the register take the same loop from the start of a shift to the end of it, with no dial anywhere within reach. The third bears on the music itself, which stops counting as an event the moment it becomes a curtain hung behind every activity. Silence is not a hole waiting to be filled. It is what makes a sound audible at all, and it deserves defending the way anything scarce deserves defending.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the tuner of the theater began his apprenticeship very early
he sorted felts in the workshop of an instrument maker
he was first taught to listen for the beats between neighboring strings
he then spent a year replacing hammers
he also set the travel of every key on the keyboard
once he was a tuner he made the rounds of concert halls
the heat of the stage lights threatens the steadiness of the instrument
he says one wrong note is enough to shake the confidence of an orchestra
he now passes his trade on to two apprentices
text: The tuner who works for the theater started young, in the workshop of an instrument maker who had him sorting felts. Long before anyone handed him a key, he was taught to listen for the beats that rise between two strings tuned close together. A whole year then went on swapping out hammers and setting the travel of every key on the keyboard, fussy work that asks for a hand which never wavers. Once he had the trade, he followed it through concert halls, where an instrument has to hold steady against the heat pouring off the lights and the air a full house stirs up. One sour note, he says, heard from the stands, is enough to shake the confidence of a whole orchestra. He now teaches two apprentices, telling them that the ear is built by patience, and that the hand follows on after.

units: the concert under review took place in an old covered market
the metal roof and the concrete floor throw the sound back hard
this layout gives a tinny return
the trio cut its volume to suit the place
the gaps left between musical phrases became noticeable
the double bass suffered from too much low end in that space
the drums on the other hand gained from the acoustics
the reviewer advises standing close to the stage
text: Honestly, the show in the old covered market was worth the trip, and what stayed with me had as much to do with the building as with the playing. Sheet metal overhead, raw concrete underfoot: every note comes straight back at you with a tinny edge, which means a loud band would turn to mush in there within a minute. The trio had clearly worked this out. They played soft, then softer, and the gaps between the phrases ended up carrying as much weight as the notes did. The double bass took the worst of it, since low frequencies gather in a shed like that and thicken into a paste. The drums came out ahead: each stroke shot up into the roof beams and came back wider than it left. One tip if you go. Stand down front, right against the platform, or what you hear will be roof and metal and very little of the players.
